analogy.p: The Witches are like a fortune-teller who hands a person a sentence with half of it blanked out. The person fills in the blank with what they most want; the fortune-teller did not write it, yet it would not have been written without them. The analogy breaks down because the Witches also appear to know the future, which a fortune-teller does not.
analogy.t: The fortune-teller and the empty page

bullets: They appear in Act 1 Sc 1, Act 1 Sc 3 and Act 4 Sc 1, and are discussed or recalled in other scenes (for example in Lady Macbeth's letter in Act 1 Sc 5 and Macbeth's reproach in Act 5 Sc 8). A further scene with Hecate (Act 3 Sc 5) is thought by many editors to have been added by another playwright, so be cautious about building an argument only on it.
Dramatic functions: opening hook; supernatural atmosphere; the catalyst for the plot; a source of dramatic irony; an image of moral and natural disorder.

They are never explained: Shakespeare does not tell us whether they are devils, goddesses of destiny, or village witches. The ambiguity allows several interpretations, which is useful for a grade 9 answer.
They speak in a distinctive verse (short rhyming lines) that sets them apart from the blank verse of the noble characters, so their speech sounds like a chant or spell.
The Witches are associated with paradox: they say fair is foul and foul is fair, and their prophecies are both true and false.

callouts.p: From Old English wyrd, fate or destiny. In the play the Weird Sisters are linked to fate, but the word also carries the modern sense of strange and unnatural.
Do not begin with what the witches look like. Begin with what they do to the play: unsettle the audience, plant an idea, and test Macbeth. Then use language and structure to prove it.
callouts.t: Start from effect, not from description

core.h: Who they are and what they do in the play
core.p: The three Witches, called the Weird Sisters in the text, are the first characters the audience sees and the most mysterious. Their word weird comes from the Old English wyrd, meaning fate, which suggests they are connected with destiny rather than being ordinary women. They do not control events directly; they speak prophecies, tempt, and disturb. Their dramatic function is to set the tone of the play (disorder, supernatural menace, ambiguity), to supply the trigger for Macbeth's ambition, and to create suspense because the audience wants to know how the prophecies will be fulfilled.

bullets: The scene is set on a heath, in thunder and lightning: pathetic fallacy of nature reflecting moral disorder, and a signal that normal rules do not apply.

The Witches speak in rhyming couplets and short trochaic lines (stress on the first syllable), which produce a chanting, spell-like rhythm quite different from the iambic pentameter of Duncan and the nobles.

"Fair is foul, and foul is fair" is a chiasmus (the words reverse in order) and a paradox. The balance of the line sounds like a spell and shows that moral categories will be inverted in the world of the play.
They refer to animal familiars, Graymalkin and Paddock, which belong to the Jacobean image of witches as women who keep demonic spirits in the shape of cats and toads.
The scene ends with the line "Hover through the fog and filthy air": the adjectives and the sibilance create a polluted atmosphere, and the verb ‘hover’ suggests an uncanny movement between worlds.
The very short length is a structural decision: the audience has a fragment of prophecy and a name, Macbeth, before anything else, so we associate him with the supernatural before we meet him.

callouts.p: In Act 1 Sc 3 Macbeth's first words are that he has not seen so foul and fair a day. The echo connects him with the Witches before he has met them, and many critics read it as a sign that his mind is already attuned to their language.
callouts.t: Fair is foul: echoed by Macbeth

core.h: Act 1 Sc 1: the opening and the paradox of fair and foul
core.p: The play begins with a very short scene: three Witches arrange to meet Macbeth after the battle, in thunder and lightning. There is no exposition about who they are; Shakespeare drops us into a world of storm and mystery. The scene is only a few lines but it establishes the whole moral landscape of the play. The opening question about when they will meet again, asked in the first line, is answered by a plan to meet ‘ere the set of sun’, while the closing couplet states that fair is foul, and foul is fair. This paradox, repeated later by Macbeth himself, sets up the central theme of appearance and reality.

head: Feature
Example
Effect
rows: Sounds like a spell; contrasts with the noble characters' iambic verse
Fair is foul, and foul is fair
Moral inversion; the key idea of the play
Nature reflects the arrival of evil
Jacobean beliefs about witches' animal spirits

bullets: The Witches' revenge on the sailor's wife shows petty, spiteful malice; the line ‘Aroint thee, witch!’ shows that the people of the play are afraid of them.

Banquo's first reaction is suspicion and fear: he says that they do not look like the inhabitants of the earth and that their beards forbid him to interpret them as women. His observation suggests a challenge to the Great Chain of Being and to gender order.
Macbeth, in contrast, starts, and Banquo notices, asking why he seems to fear things that sound so fair. The question hints at something in Macbeth's mind that Banquo does not share.

Macbeth's aside begins with two truths told as prologues to a great theme; he feels a horrid image unfix his hair and reflects that present fears are less than horrible imaginings. His imagination is already travelling to murder.

Macbeth also tells himself that chance may crown him without his stir; for a moment he thinks fate will do the work. Seconds later the idea of murder returns. This is the key evidence for the debate about free will.

Banquo warns that the instruments of darkness tell us truths, win us with honest trifles, to betray us in deepest consequence. The warning gives the audience a model of the right response, and Macbeth's failure to follow it is his choice.

callouts.p: The Witches say Macbeth will be king; they never tell him to murder Duncan. That decision comes from Macbeth and Lady Macbeth. Say this explicitly if you argue about responsibility.
callouts.t: The prophecy does not tell him to kill

core.h: Act 1 Sc 3: the prophecies and the first reaction
core.p: In Act 1 Sc 3 the Witches boast about their petty cruelty (one has been killing swine, another tells of a sailor's wife who refused her chestnuts and called her ‘rump-fed ronyon’) and promise to torment the sailor, whose sleep will not rest on his ‘penthouse lid’. The scene is an example of the Jacobean idea that witches avenge small slights through malice. When Macbeth and Banquo arrive, the sisters greet Macbeth as Thane of Glamis, Thane of Cawdor, and ‘king hereafter’, and tell Banquo that he will be lesser and greater than Macbeth, not so happy yet much happier, and that he will get kings though he be none.

head: Prophecy
To whom
Fulfilment
rows: Already true (he is Glamis by inheritance)
Confirmed within the scene when Ross and Angus arrive
Fulfilled only after Duncan is murdered
Banquo is not king but his line will be
Not so happy, yet much happier
He dies, but his descendants rule
Thou shalt get kings, though thou be none
Open at the end; Fleance escapes

bullets: The chanting refrain "Double, double toil and trouble; / Fire burn and cauldron bubble" is rhythmic and incantatory; the repeated sounds make it memorable and ritualistic, almost like a nursery rhyme turned sinister.

The catalogue of ingredients uses animal and human parts (including parts of outsiders, which reflects Jacobean prejudice), which would have repelled the audience; the grotesque list stresses the unnatural and corrupt nature of their craft.
Macbeth now seeks them out: the power relationship has changed from Act 1, when they met him. He is no longer reacting but depending on them.
The apparitions play on his hopes: an armed head, a bloody child and a crowned child holding a tree are symbols of violence, birth and succession. They are also riddles that he reads as comfort.
Macbeth says he will make assurance double sure and take a bond of fate, deciding to kill Macduff anyway; he does not trust his own reading of the prophecy, a sign of his escalating paranoia.

The show of eight kings and the sight of Banquo, ‘blood-boltered’, smiling at him shows that Banquo's line will rule; Macbeth's response is rage, and his decision to attack Macduff's family follows immediately.

callouts.p: Using words that have two meanings, so that a statement is technically true but misleads the listener. Macbeth uses the word to condemn the Witches when he realises he has been deceived.
Macbeth hears the good news and ignores the warning. The structure of the scene (a warning first, then two reassurances) shows that he fixes on what he wants to hear.
callouts.t: The apparitions and Macbeth's tragic error

core.h: Act 4 Sc 1: the cauldron and the apparitions
core.p: In Act 4 Sc 1 the Witches gather round a cauldron, chanting the famous "Double, double toil and trouble", and throw in a catalogue of grotesque ingredients (eye of newt, toe of frog, and the finger of a birth-strangled babe). The scene is the climax of the supernatural plot. Macbeth, now king and insecure, goes to find them, calls them "secret, black, and midnight hags", and demands answers. They offer to answer through their masters, and three apparitions appear: an armed head warns him to beware Macduff; a bloody child tells him that none of woman born shall harm him; a crowned child holding a tree says he will not be vanquished until Birnam Wood comes to Dunsinane.

bullets: Fate reading: the Witches know the future and Macbeth cannot escape it. Evidence: the prophecy of Cawdor is fulfilled at once; the weird sisters are linked to wyrd and fate.
Temptation reading: the Witches offer, Macbeth chooses. Evidence: no instruction to murder; ‘chance may crown me’ suggests he considers a passive path; Banquo's resistance.
Psychological reading: the Witches externalise Macbeth's desires. Evidence: his rapid shift into thoughts of murder in his aside; his letter to Lady Macbeth shows that he told his wife at once.
Modern reading: audiences may see the Witches as a satire of fear; Jacobean audiences may have seen them as real. A reading must say which audience it describes.
The Witches also create dramatic irony because they know, as the audience does, that the prophecies will not bring happiness.

callouts.p: That claim is too simple. Say they act as catalysts or tempters, then use evidence of Macbeth's own choices (Act 1 Sc 7, Act 2 Sc 1) to argue that he is responsible.
callouts.t: Do not say the Witches made him do it

fig.cap: Weigh the readings; the best answers argue for the middle one while conceding the others.

core.p: One of the most important grade 9 skills is to offer more than one interpretation. The Witches can be read as agents of fate, as tempters who cannot compel, or as projections of Macbeth's own ambition. A good answer will weigh them rather than pick one without evidence. The strongest middle position is that the Witches supply the spark but Macbeth supplies the fuel: they cannot act without his co-operation, and Banquo hears the same prophecy and refuses to commit a crime.

bullets: Rhyming couplets: unlike the nobles' blank verse, rhyme gives the Witches a sing-song sound which is both comic and chilling.
Paradox and inversion: fair is foul; lesser and greater; not so happy yet much happier. The structure of their speech mirrors the moral confusion they create.
Imperatives and spells: verbs like ‘hover’, ‘toil’, ‘bubble’ and ‘burn’ create a sense of ritual action.
Dramatic irony: the audience knows (from Act 1 Sc 1) that the Witches plan to meet Macbeth, so every prophecy is heard through a lens of suspicion.

Staging: thunder, lightning, a cauldron, a trapdoor for the apparitions. Jacobean theatres had stage machinery that would have made the supernatural vivid; modern productions often use sound and lighting to keep the same effect.
Contrast: the Witches deliver riddles; Lady Macbeth delivers commands; Macbeth speaks in soliloquies. These different types of speech show who has power over whom.
core.p: Shakespeare gives the Witches a particular voice that works against the grand blank verse of the court. They speak mostly in trochaic tetrameter, with strong first stresses, rhyming couplets, and repeated sounds. This creates a chant-like, almost childlike rhythm that makes them seem both playful and menacing. They also communicate through riddles, paradox and ambiguous statements, so that language itself becomes a form of deception. Structurally, their scenes frame the play: the opening scene sets in motion the plot and the Act 4 scene tests Macbeth at the point of greatest confidence.

head: Scene
Key language feature
Effect
rows: Establishes a world where values are reversed
Menace plus temptation; contrast with Banquo's scepticism
Spectacle and riddling language confirm Macbeth's doom

bullets: The belief that witches could raise storms is echoed in the Witches' threat to torment the sailor with tempests; this would have reminded James of his own experience.

Witches were often old, poor women accused of malice, which fits Banquo's description of them as "withered and so wild". Modern audiences may feel sympathy for them as outcasts; Jacobean audiences were more likely to fear them.
The idea of a world turned upside down (witches, a murdered king, unnatural omens) reflects Jacobean fear of rebellion against divinely ordered hierarchy.
Banquo was believed to be an ancestor of James; the prophecy that his line will rule flatters the king and gives the Witches' prophecy a political edge.
Be careful with historical statements: say "James I wrote about witchcraft" and "the 1604 Witchcraft Act", and avoid exact numbers of trials or victims unless you are sure.

callouts.p: Instead of a separate paragraph on witches in history, tie context to a quotation. For example: when Banquo describes the sisters as unlike the inhabitants of the earth, a Jacobean audience, schooled by King James's Daemonologie, would hear a warning about unnatural, diabolical powers.

core.h: Context (AO3): James I, witchcraft and the Jacobean mind
core.p: Macbeth was written for James I, who was the author of Daemonologie (1597), a book on witchcraft, and who believed that he had been the target of witches in the North Berwick trials in Scotland in the early 1590s, in which people were accused of raising storms to endanger his voyage. Soon after he became King of England in 1603, a new Witchcraft Act (1604) made the crime harsher. Audiences in 1606 would have taken the Witches seriously as a real threat, and would have been fascinated and horrified by the supernatural. Shakespeare also used Holinshed's Chronicles, which describes the weird sisters as figures connected with destiny.

bullets: Macbeth: the Witches shape his psychology: from ambition to dependence to disillusion.
Banquo: his reaction is the foil; he sees the same sisters and chooses to doubt them.

Lady Macbeth: she invokes spirits herself in Act 1 Sc 5 (to unsex her), and Macbeth's letter to her reports that the Witches have more in them than mortal knowledge, so she receives the prophecy second-hand and turns it into a plan.
Macduff: the Witches' prophecy about Macduff leads Macbeth to destroy his family, but Macduff becomes the instrument of the final reversal.
The Porter: his speech on equivocation in Act 2 Sc 3 mirrors the Witches' double meanings and lets the audience see that the whole play is full of ambiguous language.

callouts.p: The play moves from prophecy (Act 1) to testing and misreading (Act 4) to recognition (Act 5). This framework turns the Witches into a structural device as well as characters.

fig.cap: The Witches' scenes mark the play's turning points; Macbeth moves from being approached to seeking them out.

core.h: Links to other themes and characters
core.p: The Witches connect to almost every major idea in the play. They are the embodiment of appearance and reality because their words seem fair but are foul. They underpin ambition and fate versus free will by posing the question of how far Macbeth is responsible. They link to the unnatural because their appearances coincide with storms and disorder. They also contrast with the other voices in the play: Banquo's wise caution, Lady Macbeth's powerful decisiveness, and the Porter's comic equivocation.

bullets: In an extract question on Act 1 Sc 1 or Act 4 Sc 1, comment on sound (rhyme, rhythm, repetition), imagery (grotesque ingredients, fog), and structure (short opening, escalating apparitions).
In an (b) question on responsibility, plan a balanced thesis: the Witches are catalysts, but Macbeth chooses.
Use short, accurate quotations. Good flexible choices are "fair is foul, and foul is fair", ‘juggling fiends’ and "palter with us in a double sense".
Link every point to the whole play: opening hook, central temptation, climactic false reassurance, final realisation.
Write about the effect on the audience: fear, suspense, dramatic irony.
Avoid the claim that the Witches are simply comic or simply evil; show the range of tones.

callouts.p: A grade 9 answer uses context to illuminate the text, not to excuse it. Context should deepen the reading of an image, not replace analysis.
callouts.t: Do not treat them as only a Jacobean curiosity

core.h: Exam technique: writing about the Witches
core.p: Questions on the Witches usually ask how they are presented in an extract and elsewhere, or how far they are responsible for Macbeth's actions. A strong answer will use specific language and structure to show how Shakespeare creates the supernatural atmosphere and how he leaves their nature ambiguous. Integrate AO3 into your argument, offer at least two interpretations, and end by saying what Shakespeare achieves through them. Check the marks and timings printed on your paper for the exact breakdown of the assessment objectives.

plan: Structure and language of the cauldron scene: chant, grotesque catalogue, reversal of power.
The apparitions: how each plays on his hopes; equivocation.
Elsewhere: the opening and Act 1 Sc 3; Banquo as foil.
Context: James I, witchcraft and the Jacobean audience.
Conclusion: the Witches reveal the tragedy of misplaced trust.
essays.q: Explore how Shakespeare presents the Witches and their influence on Macbeth in Act 4 Sc 1 and elsewhere in the play.
essays.text:
Shakespeare presents the Witches as ambiguous catalysts: they do not force Macbeth to act, but their riddling language exposes the flaws that he brings to them. In Act 4 Sc 1 the balance of power has reversed, and the man who was once met on the heath now goes to meet them, and his dependence is the measure of his fall.

The scene begins with a chant, "Double, double toil and trouble", whose doubling and heavy rhyme turn the stage into a ritual space. The sound is playful, almost a nursery rhyme, and that is its menace: the language of hardship is made domestic, and the catalogue of ingredients that follows, with the eye of newt and the finger of a birth-strangled babe, is a grotesque list of bodies broken for a spell. For a Jacobean audience that had been schooled by King James's writing on witchcraft, the effect would have been of an authentic and horrifying ritual, a sign that the natural order had been inverted. Yet the rhythm also separates the Witches from the noble blank verse and so frames them as a different order of being.

Macbeth's arrival turns the scene. He calls them "secret, black, and midnight hags", words that condemn them, and yet he asks them for answers. Here Shakespeare uses the characters' verbal dynamics: the king commands but pleads in the same breath. The three apparitions are a masterpiece of equivocation. The armed head warns him to beware Macduff, and Macbeth responds by thinking of killing; the bloody child says that none of woman born shall harm him, and Macbeth reads this as immunity; the crowned child with the tree promises safety until Birnam Wood moves, and Macbeth dismisses it as impossible. The structure is a warning followed by two reassurances, and Macbeth fastens on the comforting words and discards the warning. The prophecies are true to the ear and false to the hope, a phrase he will later use to condemn the ‘juggling fiends’.

But Shakespeare also makes the audience question who is deceiving whom. Banquo's earlier warning that the "instruments of darkness tell us truths" gave the audience a model of the right response, and Banquo, hearing the same prophecy, stayed loyal. The Witches never tell Macbeth to kill Duncan; the closest they come is to hail him as king hereafter. His aside in Act 1 Sc 3 shows a mind already turning to murder, and his decision, after the apparitions, to make assurance double sure by killing Macduff's family shows that he still acts from fear. In that light, the Witches resemble a mirror: they offer an image, and Macbeth sees himself.

The play's structure supports this reading. The opening scene, only a few lines long, establishes that fair is foul and foul is fair, a paradox that Macbeth himself echoes in his first line. By Act 4 the paradox has become a method: the prophecies are fair on the surface and foul beneath. By Act 5 Macbeth sees that the fiends "palter with us in a double sense", but even this recognition has an edge of evasion, because he has no one else to blame.

Shakespeare's purpose, therefore, is not to excuse Macbeth by supernatural force, nor to dismiss the Witches as superstition. He uses them to dramatise a Jacobean anxiety: that evil can speak truth in order to deceive, and that a man who is eager to be deceived will be.
essays.thesis: Shakespeare presents the Witches as ambiguous catalysts whose riddling language exposes rather than creates Macbeth's flaws: they give shape to his desire, but his choices make him their victim.
why: AO1: a clear, conceptual thesis (catalysts, mirror, misplaced trust) is sustained and developed throughout, with a balanced use of interpretations.
AO2: close analysis of rhythm, doubling, equivocation and structure (warning followed by two reassurances; the short opening scene).
AO3: context (James I, Jacobean witchcraft beliefs) is integrated into the analysis of the chant and the ritual, rather than added as a separate paragraph.
The essay moves between the extract and the whole play, tracking how the same idea develops from Act 1 to Act 5.
Alternative readings (fate, temptation, mirror) are weighed and a judgment is reached.

model: Thesis: the Witches are presented as ambiguous, unsettling figures who tempt but never command.
Banquo's description (beards, unlike inhabitants of the earth) creates unnatural, disorienting imagery.
Paradox and riddling prophecy: lesser and greater; not so happy yet much happier.
Macbeth's start and aside versus Banquo's scepticism: the Witches test character.
Link to the opening (fair is foul) and Act 4 Sc 1 apparitions.
AO3: James I and witchcraft beliefs; weird as fate.
Structure: the prophecy is confirmed at once (Cawdor), which makes the audience, and Macbeth, trust the rest.
exam.q: Read the extract from Act 1 Sc 3 (the Witches greet Macbeth and Banquo). Explore how Shakespeare presents the Witches in this extract and in the play as a whole. (40 marks including AO4; check the marks on your paper)
exam.tip: Include at least one point from outside the extract; analyse a single word such as start, horrid or fair.

model: Agree: they plant the idea; prophecies are fulfilled; the apparitions give false confidence.
Disagree: no instruction to kill; Banquo's contrasting choice; Macbeth's aside and soliloquies show his own ambition.
Lady Macbeth's role: she turns the prophecy into a plan.
Equivocation: the Witches deceive but Macbeth chooses to trust.
Structure: frame of prophecy (Acts 1 and 4) and recognition (Act 5 Sc 8).
AO3: Jacobean belief in witchcraft and in free will.
Judgment: catalysts, not causes.
exam.q: How far do you agree that the Witches are responsible for Macbeth's downfall? (40 marks for a (b) style question; check your paper)
exam.tip: State your line of argument in the first paragraph and keep returning to it.

model: Thunder and lightning; the heath: pathetic fallacy.
Rhyming, chanting trochaic rhythm.
Paradox: fair is foul, and foul is fair.
Familiars: Graymalkin and Paddock.
Brevity and lack of exposition.
Fog and filthy air: sensory imagery.
exam.q: Explain how Shakespeare creates a sense of the supernatural in Act 1 Sc 1. (10 marks, approximate)
exam.tip: Use the pattern feature, example, effect for each paragraph.

model: Armed head: beware Macduff; Macbeth ignores the warning's implication.
Bloody child: none of woman born; he trusts it literally.
Crowned child with the tree: Birnam Wood; he sees impossibility.
Equivocation: riddles hide a second meaning.
Reveals Macbeth's dependence and arrogance: he seeks reassurance.
Foreshadows his overthrow and his later recognition in Act 5 Sc 8.
exam.q: Write about the Witches' apparitions in Act 4 Sc 1 and what they reveal about Macbeth. (12 marks, approximate)
exam.tip: Name the technique (equivocation) and explain what the audience understands that Macbeth does not.

model: For: they frame the play and begin the plot; their language sets the theme of appearance and reality.
Against: Macbeth and Lady Macbeth drive the action; the Witches appear in only a few scenes.
Their influence is more through ideas than action.
Link to other characters: Banquo, Macduff, Lady Macbeth.
Judgment: essential as a structural and thematic device even if not the cause.
exam.q: "The Witches are the most important characters in the play." How far do you agree? (20 marks, approximate)
exam.tip: Give a clear judgment, not just a list.

model: Thesis: Shakespeare presents a world where the supernatural offers fate but humans choose.
Paragraph 1: Act 1 Sc 3 prophecy and Macbeth's aside.
Paragraph 2: Banquo as foil: same prophecy, different choice.
Paragraph 3: Act 4 Sc 1 apparitions and equivocation.
Paragraph 4: Context: Jacobean views of providence and witchcraft.
Conclusion: tragedy arises from choice, not compulsion.
exam.q: Plan an answer (5 minutes) on "Fate and free will in Macbeth". (Planning task)
exam.tip: One quotation and one structural point per paragraph.

model: Act 1 Sc 1: brief, mysterious, paradox, they plan to meet Macbeth.
Act 4 Sc 1: elaborate ritual, cauldron, apparitions; Macbeth seeks them.
Power shift: in Act 1 they meet him; in Act 4 he comes to them.
Language: couplets in both; Act 4 adds the catalogue and the chant.
Tone shift from menace to spectacle and doom.
exam.q: Compare how Shakespeare presents the Witches in Act 1 Sc 1 and Act 4 Sc 1. (12 marks, approximate)
exam.tip: Use comparative connectives such as whereas and in contrast.

mistakes.r: They offer prophecy; the decision to murder is Macbeth's and Lady Macbeth's. Use the aside and Banquo's contrast as evidence.
mistakes.w: Saying the Witches make Macbeth kill Duncan.

mistakes.r: Analyse how Shakespeare uses rhythm, paradox and ambiguity to create unease, and link to Jacobean beliefs.
mistakes.w: Describing the Witches as just ‘ugly old women’.

mistakes.r: Their statements are technically true; the deception lies in equivocation and in Macbeth's misreading.
Comment on the placement of the opening scene, the escalation of the apparitions and the final recognition in Act 5 Sc 8.
Link a specific image (for example the storm raised against the sailor) to James's beliefs and to the effect on the audience.
mistakes.w: Tacking on context ("James I believed in witches").

mistakes.r: Use two or three words and zoom in on sound or imagery.
mistakes.w: Quoting long chunks of the cauldron chant from memory.

mistakes.r: Distinguish them: a warning, two reassurances, and the show of kings; explain how each plays on Macbeth's mind.
mistakes.w: Saying all the apparitions are the same.

mistakes.r: Argue about balance: the Witches are catalysts; Macbeth has choice, as the contrast with Banquo shows.
mistakes.w: Writing that Macbeth has no free will.

quotes.a: The chiasmus and the balanced rhythm make the line sound like a spell. By reversing fair and foul, the Witches announce that moral categories will be inverted, which is exactly what happens when a loyal general becomes a murderer. It also offers a thematic key: appearances throughout the play will deceive.
quotes.c: Jacobean fear of hidden evil behind fair appearances
quotes.q: Fair is foul, and foul is fair

quotes.a: The imperative verb and the polluted adjectives create an atmosphere of dirt and confusion. The alliteration of the f sounds gives a sinister whisper, and the idea of hovering suggests they exist between worlds, neither fully natural nor fully diabolical. Placing the line at the end of the first scene sets the tone for the whole play.
quotes.c: Witches associated with storms and disorder
quotes.q: Hover through the fog and filthy air

quotes.a: The sailor's wife is quoted as shouting a curse at the Witch. The line shows ordinary people fearing and rejecting witches, and gives the First Witch a petty, vengeful motive. It makes the sisters sound both malicious and absurdly small-scale, which contrasts with the epic ambitions they stir in Macbeth.
quotes.c: Accusations of witchcraft against poor women

quotes.a: The Witch promises that sleep will not rest on the sailor's eyelid. The word penthouse means a sloping roof, so the eyelid becomes a shelter that sleep cannot cling to. Sleeplessness is also one of Macbeth's later torments, so the line foreshadows the effect of guilt through a curse on another man.
quotes.c: Witches believed able to inflict illness and torment

quotes.a: Banquo sees the sisters as unnatural: they look like women but have beards. The line challenges gender categories and suggests a disruption of nature that matches their moral threat. Banquo's careful, sceptical language shows the sensible response that Macbeth will fail to copy.
quotes.c: Great Chain of Being; anxiety about women who defy roles
quotes.q: your beards forbid me to interpret

quotes.a: The paradox is a perfect piece of riddling speech: both parts are true, but in different ways. Banquo will not be king, yet his descendants will be. The structure of the line, reversing expectation within a few words, anticipates the double meanings of later prophecies.
quotes.c: Banquo as ancestor of James I

quotes.a: Banquo warns that evil may tell the truth in order to deceive. The metaphor of instruments suggests that the Witches are used by a higher power, while darkness has moral and visual meaning. The line gives the audience the moral lens through which to judge Macbeth's decision to listen.
quotes.c: Jacobean belief in devils who use truth to tempt
quotes.q: The instruments of darkness tell us truths

quotes.a: The doubling in the first word and the chanting rhythm give the line the quality of a charm. The words toil and trouble sound like everyday hardship, which makes the horror domestic; the repeated sound makes the line unforgettable. It also echoes the doubleness at the heart of the prophecies: everything has two meanings.
quotes.c: Popular belief in spells and incantations

quotes.a: The Witch recognises Macbeth's approach by a prickling in her thumbs and calls him something wicked. This reversal is striking: the evil beings call the human visitor wicked, which shows how far he has fallen. The vague noun something increases the sense of unease and makes Macbeth seem less than fully human.

The apparition's promise sounds absolute, but it hides a loophole: a man born by Caesarean section is not born in the usual way. The line is a clear example of equivocation, and Macbeth's confidence in it leads him to relax at precisely the moment he should be most alert.
quotes.c: Prophecy and riddle in Jacobean drama
quotes.q: none of woman born / Shall harm Macbeth

quotes.a: The noun phrase compares the Witches to conjurors who play tricks with words and appearances. Macbeth's anger shows that he finally understands the equivocation, but the phrase also tries to blame the fiends for his own choices. It is both a recognition and an evasion.

To palter means to speak deceitfully or trifle; the phrase describes how the prophecies kept the word of promise to the ear and broke it to the hope. This is Macbeth's last chance to name the pattern of the play, and the language is suddenly clear and exact, as if he has finally escaped his own illusions.
quotes.q: palter with us in a double sense

summary: The Witches (the Weird Sisters) open the play, deliver the prophecies that ignite Macbeth's ambition, and return in Act 4 with the apparitions that make him over-confident. For Edexcel you need to explain their dramatic function, how Shakespeare's language and structure make them unsettling, how far they cause Macbeth's fall, and how Jacobean beliefs about witchcraft shape the audience's response (AO3).

terms.d: Speaking in a way that is deliberately ambiguous or misleading while remaining technically true.
A line of four feet, each with a stressed syllable followed by an unstressed one; the Witches' chanting rhythm.
A statement that appears self-contradictory but contains a truth, such as fair is foul.
A structure in which words are repeated in reverse order, as in fair is foul and foul is fair.
Nature mirroring the mood or events of the story, as in the thunder and lightning of the opening scene.
Beyond the natural world; the Witches and the apparitions.
The question of whether events are predetermined or caused by human choice.
In Jacobean belief, an animal spirit that served a witch, such as Graymalkin the cat.
When the audience knows something characters do not.
A speech heard by the audience but not by other characters on stage.
